title: Git-backed Performance Profile Change Proposal, Validation, and Review Flow
creator: Priya Sinha
description: Establish a Git-backed change proposal and review workflow for Redwood-verified performance profiles (latency, throughput, cost). Current profile updates are handled through a mix of manual steps and ad-hoc scripts. This ticket defines the product and process requirements for a reproducible, auditable change flow: proposals are authored as profile change documents in a canonical repo, CI executes automated validation (benchmarks and compatibility checks), reviewers (PM/Eng/Runtime) leave structured feedback, and a signed profile manifest is produced for publishing to the profile registry. Goal: reduce friction for model onboarding and accelerations while improving auditability and enabling safe rollbacks.
acceptance_criteria: Canonical Git repo (profiles.redwood.ai/profiles) exists with CONTRIBUTING.md describing change proposal format and required metadata
CI job that runs synthetic latency/throughput/cost benchmarks for proposed profile changes and returns pass/fail status on PR within 2 hours
Automatic compatibility check ensures proposed profile matches supported model architecture and quantization level (failure yields actionable CI output)
Reviewer checklist implemented as PR templates and enforcable branch protections requiring sign-off from at least one PM and one Runtime engineer

On merge, an automated process produces a signed performance manifest (JSON) and updates the profile registry with a new version string; a canary publish mode available to limit exposure to a subset of customers
Rollback path documented and tested: the system can revert to previous signed manifest and trigger an automated invalidation of caches within 30 minutes
Operational playbook pages updated (Confluence) with troubleshooting steps and SLOs for profile validation CI
tasks: Design PR change format for 'performance-profile.md' including fields: model_id, model_version, hardware_profile, dataset_signature, latency_p50/p90, throughput, token_cost_estimate, recommended_quantization
Create profiles.redwood.ai Git repo and initial branch structure (proposals, accepted, archived)
Implement CI harness to run the verified-benchmark pipeline (reuse ENG/bench runner) against PR commits and publish artifacts to the PR checks
Add PR templates and set branch protection rules requiring labels and sign-offs
Build automation to generate signed manifest on merge and push to internal registry endpoint and S3 bucket
Implement canary publish toggle in registry and Console to limit serving of new profiles to dedicated test tenants
Write rollback automation and test end-to-end revert scenario
Author Confluence operational playbook and runbook for incidents related to profile regressions
links: https://console.redwood.ai/dashboards/perf-profiles (dashboard to show publish history and canary percentage)
notes: Rationale: moving to Git-backed proposals provides cryptographic provenance, easier rollback, and enables smaller teams (research/partner integrators) to submit candidate profiles via PRs.
We will not replace the UI publishing experience on Day 1; initial flow is Git-first with Console integration planned in a follow-up ticket.
Bench harness should attempt to reproduce customer-like tail latency by using request distribution traces from Console aggregated samples (anonymized).
Canary publish should default to 0% and require a manual increase via Console or API; telemetry must show no >5% increase in 99th percentile latency for canary tenants before raising exposure.
Signing keys for manifests will be managed by an automation service account; rotation policy documented in ops playbook.

implementation_notes: Keep the profile file format simple (YAML or markdown frontmatter) to make it human-editable.
CI must produce a small artifacts page with plots: latency histogram, p50/p90/p99 comparison, throughput curve, and per-token cost estimate.
Profiles should include a 'validation_seed' to allow deterministic microbench runs for reproducibility.
Consider a short-lived 'staging registry' for merged but not-yet-signed manifests to allow additional automated gating steps.
